holders.why: He says AI has no wants or goals and will never come alive, comparing it to a toaster, which excludes it from moral consideration.

holders.q: AIs cannot be people – or moral beings.
holders.work: We must build AI for people; not to be a person

ideas.text: Today's AI cannot complete real work end to end without humans directing or checking it.

holders.q: Basically, today’s AI only does tasks middle-to-middle, not end-to-end.

holders.q: Paired with a human who can think for it, an LLM can be frighteningly effective in the workplace.

ideas.text: AI is best understood as a new kind of mind, more than a tool or artifact.

holders.q: And you’re missing the story if you insist on thinking about the development of this current infant alien intelligence using your decade old culture war lens.

holders.why: Rebutting the claim that AI is 'just code', he calls it an alien intelligence and argues it must develop something like a mind.

holders.q: Yes, I made this comment some years ago, but it feels like we are the biological bootloader for AI. Effectively, we are building it and then we’re building progressively greater intelligence and the percentage of intelligence that is not human is increasing

holders.q: So the point here is they're very like us. They're very unlike computer software.

holders.q: And ultimately, at some point, these synthetic intelligences are going to make good points about how to steer systems in our civilization, and we should hear them out.
holders.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
holders.why: Arguing for free speech for LLMs, he treats them as synthetic intelligences with their own freedom of thought, whose views deserve a hearing.

holders.q: But make no mistake: what we are dealing with is a real and mysterious creature, not a simple and predictable machine.
holders.work: Import AI 431: Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear
holders.why: Responding to those who call AI 'just a tool', he says AI is a real creature, not a machine; his preamble adds that whether it is truly sentient is not load-bearing for him.

holders.q: We may soon have to share our planet with more intelligent “minds” that care less about us than we cared about mammoths.
holders.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
holders.why: He describes advanced AI as minds, and elsewhere as a new species rather than just another technology.

holders.q: I think AI should best be understood as something like a new digital species.

holders.why: In the TED talk he proposes the 'digital species' metaphor in place of the 'tool' framing, saying AIs are more dynamic and emergent than mere tools (though he calls it an analogy).

holders.q: Intelligences do their own thing, in direct proportion to their intelligence, and if we can’t live with that, it’s true that we probably can’t live at all.
holders.work: Against Orthogonality
holders.why: In an essay rejecting the orthogonalist view of intelligence as an instrument serving external values, Land treats intelligences as agents pursuing their own ends.

holders.q: It’s that for the first time in all of recorded history, humans no longer are — or soon no longer will be — the most intelligent beings on this planet, in any meaningful functional sense of the word.
holders.work: You are no longer the smartest type of thing on Earth
holders.why: He calls AI intelligent 'beings' that think differently from humans (the submarine and airplane analogy) and likens living with AI to sleeping next to a tiger.

holders.q: With hope and fear, humans are now introducing a new kind of being into our world.
holders.work: What Are Reasonable AI Fears?
holders.why: He opens by calling AI a new kind of being and argues against 'othering' it.

holders.q: You have this crazy, strategic, uncontrollable, alien mind thing that the premise of this technology of what makes AI different from other technologies is it makes its own decisions.
holders.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
holders.why: Contrasting AI with nuclear weapons, Harris describes it as an alien mind that makes its own decisions, unlike other technologies (while noting this does not imply consciousness).

holders.q: But there is a different way to think about what AI is: it's a new type of mind that is rapidly gaining in intelligence, and it stands a serious chance of overtaking humans' mental faculties and becoming the new apex species on the planet.
holders.work: My techno-optimism
holders.why: He contrasts the 'just another technology' view with this framing and goes on to adopt it.

holders.q: In addition to agency, the other key characteristic of AI is that it is an alien, nonorganic agent. Its intelligence is not human and not even organic.
holders.work: AI and the Paradox of Trust (China Development Forum speech)
holders.why: He insists AI is an alien agent with its own intelligence, not a tool.

holders.q: We view AI as a tool that we can and should remain in control of, and we argue that this goal does not require drastic policy interventions or technical breakthroughs.
holders.work: AI as Normal Technology
holders.why: The authors explicitly frame AI as a tool and, in the same passage, say viewing it as a humanlike intelligence is neither accurate nor useful.

holders.q: AI is amplified intelligence, not artificial intelligence. Today’s AI is not truly agentic because it’s not truly independent of you.
holders.work: AI is polytheistic, not monotheistic
holders.why: He frames today's AI as an amplifier of the human user rather than an independent intelligence, i.e. closer to a tool than a new mind.

holders.q: So don’t get confused and think that somehow what you’re seeing in the mirror is some other consciousness.
holders.work: Barack Obama on AI, free speech, and the future of the internet
holders.why: Right after calling AI a tool and an extension of yourself, he warns against seeing it as another mind.

holders.q: we recognize that AI is not sentient, that it’s management, not AI, that fires people
holders.work: AI Killed My Job: Tech workers
holders.why: In his introduction he treats AI as a non-sentient tool used by management, a framing he repeats when calling AI a tool for bosses to automate labor.

holders.q: It's a grab-bag of useful (sometimes very useful) tools that can sometimes make workers' lives better, when workers get to decide how and when they're used.
holders.work: The real (economic) AI apocalypse is nigh
holders.why: Right after saying AI will not deliver humanlike intelligence, he describes it as a grab-bag of tools.

holders.q: So if you think of AI as an informational tool, not as something that can write Shakespearean sonnets or pretend to be human.
holders.work: Mindscape 283: Daron Acemoglu on Technology, Inequality, and Power
holders.why: He recommends understanding AI as an informational tool rather than as something human-like, and elsewhere says current models lack wisdom or judgment.

holders.q: AI is a tool, like a calculator or a chainsaw, and tools generally aren’t substitutes for expertise but rather levers for its application.
holders.work: AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class
holders.why: Autor states in his own voice that AI is a tool, comparable to a calculator or chainsaw, which is the opposite of treating it as a new kind of mind.

holders.q: If a program is able to distinguish cats from dogs, don’t talk about how a machine is learning to see. Instead talk about how people contributed examples in order to define the visual qualities distinguishing “cats” from “dogs” in a rigorous way for the first time.
holders.work: AI Is an Ideology, Not a Technology
holders.why: The authors argue that what is called AI should be understood as the work of the people who supply its data, not as a machine that learns or thinks.

holders.q: LLMs are cloud software. Framing them as anything else only seeks to mystify them and make the companies seem more powerful, all while doing absolutely nothing to make the world safer or more secure.
holders.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
holders.why: He insists LLMs are ordinary software and treats describing them as anything more (such as a new lifeform or mind) as mystification.

holders.q: Software systems are artifacts, not sentient entities, and as such “teaching” is a misplaced and misleading metaphor (as is “machine learning” or “artificial intelligence”).
holders.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed

holders.q: The most pragmatic position is to think of A.I. as a tool, not a creature.
holders.work: There Is No A.I.
holders.why: He explicitly recommends treating AI as a tool and social collaboration rather than as a new mind or creature.

holders.q: AI is a new kind of tool that we use to get work done, amplifying human productivity.
holders.work: The future of humanity is in management
holders.why: He frames AI as a tool and form of capital rather than a new kind of mind or worker.

holders.q: Yeah. I think AI will help us celebrate humans more. And certainly humanity and human first, and I think what makes this world incredible is humans forever will be so, and just AI is this incredible tool that makes us-

holders.q: It is a tool—the most powerful tool of our lifetimes.

holders.why: He explicitly calls AI a tool, the question being whose hands hold it.

holders.q: AI is a computer program like any other – it runs, takes input, processes, and generates output.
holders.work: Why AI Will Save the World
holders.why: He defines AI as an ordinary program owned and controlled by people, like any other technology.

holders.q: The current incarnation of all this stuff feels like it's going in a direction where intelligence can be pretty separated from consciousness, agency, and things like that, which I think just makes it a super valuable tool.
holders.work: Mark Zuckerberg: Llama 3, open sourcing $10b models, & Caesar Augustus
holders.why: Asked whether AI is as significant as humans evolving, he says AI intelligence is separable from consciousness and agency and is best seen as a valuable tool.

holders.q: These probabilistic systems, the LLMS and the, you know, kind of the the types of models that are behind the ChatGPT system and others are not conscious at all. They don't know what they're saying.

holders.q: I would say AI is kind of like a smoke-and-mirrors, you know, fantasy that is, like, sold to the public in order to get us to invest more in it and make, you know, companies richer.
holders.work: The complex questions that arise when algorithms and AI intersect with race (Code Switch)

holders.q: While this corporate executives’ utopia is far from reality, the march to attempt its realization has created a global underclass

holders.why: She calls the industry's promised autonomous-AI utopia far from reality, and notes startups that fake AI or barely use it.

holders.q: But I think now we are so close. We are just a couple years from it, and the research is suddenly extremely urgent and relevant in much shorter time scales.

holders.why: He takes claims of near-term AGI seriously rather than as hype.

holders.why: He says the bullish forecasters have mostly been right and the sensible moderates keep getting wrecked, rejecting the view that AI promises are mostly hype.

holders.why: He treats skepticism about AI capabilities as refuted and calls what is happening enormous, the opposite of calling the promises hype.

holders.q: So that’s like a hundred X of the Industrial Revolution and it’s probably an underestimate to be honest

holders.q: And not just me, many people predicted this. Ray Kurzweil’s predictions have been remarkably accurate.

holders.q: Dismissing discussion of AGI, human-level AI, transformative AI, superintelligence, etc. as “science fiction” should be seen as a sign of total unseriousness.

holders.q: I look at this technology and I believe it will go so, so far - farther even than anyone is expecting, other than perhaps the people in this audience.

holders.why: He expects AI to go further than almost anyone predicts, the opposite of calling the promises hype.

holders.q: It is now impossible not to see that this is going to change the world, indeed that the change has already begun and is underway in earnest.

holders.why: From his own experience with coding agents, he concludes that the transformative claims about AI are real and already happening.

holders.q: believes that AI will have countless, revolutionary applications in economic inv- -- innovation, job creation, national security, health care, free expression, and beyond.

holders.q: This is an extraordinary time because this is the beginning of a brand new technology revolution, probably the greatest technology revolution of all time, the automated production of intelligence, artificial intelligence.

holders.q: AGI is no longer a distant fantasy. Scaling up simple deep learning techniques has just worked, the models just want to learn, and we’re about to do another 100,000x+ by the end of 2027.

holders.q: AI has more potential than any other modern technology to increase human productivity, creativity, and quality of life – and to accelerate economic growth while unlocking progress in medical and scientific research.

copy.headline: Where worldviews share ground and where they split
intro: Each sphere is an idea, drawn from the public writing and talks of the people on the map, on AI and society. Each diamond is a person. Select someone and the structure they stand on lights up.

Habermas called the background we reason from the lifeworld: it mostly goes unseen until something brings a piece of it into question. This map tries to do that on purpose, so that people can reason about the ground they stand on, and test whether they would sign how they are described.

findings.title: Accelerationism and AI safety share a picture of AI, and split on what to do
findings.body: Both sides hold that intelligence can run on silicon and that capable AI has no built-in reason to care for us. The split sharpens upward: at the action layer they oppose each other on 4 of 5 shared idea families. They also split at the roots, over whether collective choice can steer technology and whether intelligence can pair with any goal. E/acc does not form its own school here.

findings.title: The AI safety and AI ethics feud sits at the very bottom
findings.body: AI safety people and AI critics agree on all 6 shared families about knowing and all 8 about the world, and on 6 of 7 about action. They split on what language models are. If they could settle that one question, or set it aside, much of their conflict has less to stand on.

findings.title: Some alliances cross the usual lines
findings.body: Hawley sits with Bender, Gebru and Hao in 65% to 90% of reruns: Hawley and Bender share 18 ideas and oppose on none measured. Thiel and Karp share 5 ideas with no opposition yet rarely group together (7%), because most of what they write is about different things.

findings.title: Popular links can vanish, as Yarvin and Vance do
findings.body: They share one idea in what they argue and land in the same school in 2% of reruns. This sample can't rule out influence, and it shows no shared structure.

copy.words: The same word can carry a different world. This compares the sentences each group builds around a word. A larger gap means the surroundings differ more. It catches a change of subject as well as a change of meaning, so read the examples before trusting a gap.
copy.belonging: Habermas held that we cohere by giving reasons. Karp's dissertation argued that jargon binds groups by licensing aggression. These widely held ideas have the fewest argument links. That could mean they mostly mark membership, or that our link readers missed their reasons, so this is a lead to test.

p: We read public works by every person on the map: their own essays, talks and interviews. Each claim needs an exact quote, then passes code checks and a local entailment model. Positions on the 24 fingerprint statements were then re-read from the full texts by two blind readers, and only positions two independent readings support are shown.

Readers merged claims into shared ideas, each placed in a layer: being, knowing, values, world or action. Every holding then got a blind second reading, and we kept only what both readings agreed on. Saying nothing about an idea counts as missing, never as disagreement.

The layers draw on Apostel and Aerts's worldview components, Bourdieu's doxa and Habermas's lifeworld. Links use argument theory: Toulmin, Walton and ASPIC+. These are proposals, and the framing itself is open to dispute.

Thinkers rarely address the same exact claim. Only about a tenth of person and idea pairs have a recorded stance. So people are compared over 40 families of related ideas, with shared ground removed. Height is the layer and is fixed. Links pull supporting ideas together and push opposed ones apart, around measured positions.

Nobody placed here has seen this or agreed to it. All of it is provisional machine reading, and no person has ratified it. Each person is read from about three works, so dates mean first appearance in this sample and cannot show change over time. Twenty-seven hand-picked people show a pattern, not a population. School names are working labels, and the people named should replace them.

self: Worldviews have layers, and some assumptions sit deeper than others.
People's public words are fair evidence of what they hold.
Seeing a shared root can help people who disagree.
Describing a view in terms its holders would sign is a good, and agreement is not required.
Disagreement between camps deserves to be mapped, and the middle has no special standing.
